takeaways: Adsorption holds solute on pore walls; area, pore size and the type of force (physical or chemical) set how much a solid holds and how it is regenerated.
An isotherm is q against the equilibrium C at one temperature; Langmuir has a plateau q<sub>m</sub>, Freundlich does not, and both are fitted from straight-line plots.
Counter-current contact loads the adsorbent near equilibrium with the feed, so it needs far less adsorbent than one stage or cross-current stages.
A fixed bed is switched at its break point; the area above the breakthrough curve gives the solute held and the length of unused bed sets the scale-up.
Ion exchange swaps equivalents: the bed is sized on operating capacity, and regeneration needs two to three times the stoichiometric chemical.
Crystallization yield comes from a solute and water balance with saturated mother liquor; evaporation and hydrate water raise it.
Nucleation rises far more steeply with supersaturation than growth does, so low, steady supersaturation with seeds gives large crystals.
Crystallizer duty includes the heat of crystallization; a vacuum crystallizer finds its own evaporation from the energy balance.
In an MSMPR crystallizer ln n is linear in L with slope −1/(Gτ), and the dominant product size is 3Gτ.
RO pushes water against Δπ, UF sieves macromolecules and stops gaining flux at the gel point, and ED pulls ions through charged membranes with a current set by the salt removed.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the types of adsorption and adsorbents, isotherm fitting, fixed-bed breakthrough, ion-exchange principles and equipment, and a descriptive account of reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration and electrodialysis; syllabi that teach crystallization in depth add yield and heat balances, nucleation and growth, crystallizer types and the MSMPR model.

bank.q: Distinguish physical adsorption from chemisorption. Describe the commonly used industrial adsorbents, and explain how surface area and pore structure decide the capacity and rate of an adsorbent.
outline: Activated carbon, silica gel, alumina, zeolites, carbon molecular sieve, polymer adsorbents
Choice of adsorbent for a duty
answer: Adsorption. Adsorption is the holding of a solute (the adsorbate) from a gas or a liquid on the surface of a solid (the adsorbent). Unlike absorption, the solute does not enter the bulk of the solid; it stays on the walls of the pores. Adsorption releases heat, the heat of adsorption, and is reversed by heating or by lowering the pressure or concentration, which is how adsorbents are regenerated.

answer.text: Two types of adsorption.

head: Property
Physical adsorption
Chemisorption
rows: 20–40 kJ/mol, near the heat of condensation
needs activation; may rise with T at first
drying, purification, solvent recovery, air separation

answer: Why separations use physical adsorption. An adsorbent in a plant is loaded and regenerated thousands of times, so the force must be weak enough to reverse by a modest change in temperature or pressure. Chemisorption is the first step of heterogeneous catalysis rather than a separation tool.

Surface area. The loading q (mass held per mass of adsorbent) grows with the area available, so adsorbents are made with huge internal area: activated carbon 500–1500 m²/g. As a check of scale, 1000 m²/g covered by a single layer of benzene molecules (0.40 nm² each) holds 2.5 × 1021 molecules, 0.32 g per g of carbon.

Pore structure. Micropores (under 2 nm) give most of the area and hold small molecules strongly but are slow to enter and may exclude large molecules; mesopores (2–50 nm) give access and some area; macropores (over 50 nm) are the roads into the grain. The rate of uptake is set by film diffusion round the grain and pore diffusion inside it, so a good adsorbent combines micropores with a network of larger pores, and smaller grains are faster but give a higher pressure drop.

Activated carbon: charred coal, wood or coconut shell activated with steam; non-polar, so it holds organic molecules even from wet streams; used for colour, taste and odour, trace organics in water, and solvent vapour recovery.
Silica gel and activated alumina: porous SiO2 (300–800 m²/g) and Al2O3 (200–400 m²/g); polar, so they hold water and are used to dry air and gases; alumina also removes fluoride from water.

Zeolites (molecular sieves): crystalline aluminosilicates with uniform openings of 0.3–1 nm. 3A admits water but not ethanol and dries ethanol; 4A, 5A and 13X admit larger molecules. Zeolite 5A or 13X separates air by equilibrium: N2, with its larger quadrupole, is held more strongly by the cations, so O2-rich gas leaves the bed.
Carbon molecular sieve: very narrow uniform pores in which O2 diffuses faster than N2; a short pressure-swing cycle gives N2-rich product, a rate separation.
Polymeric adsorbents: porous resin beads without ionic groups, used for antibiotics and phenols; ion-exchange resins look similar but exchange ions instead.

Choosing. Polar solids for water and polar molecules, carbon for organics, zeolites where molecular size or a strong electric field decides the separation. Check: every adsorbent named above is regenerated by heat or pressure swing, which is possible only because the holding is physical.

bank.q: Derive the Langmuir isotherm, stating its assumptions. Give the Freundlich isotherm, show how the constants of each are found from data, and explain the effect of pressure and temperature on adsorption equilibrium.
outline: Limits at low and high C
Effect of partial pressure and temperature
answer: Assumptions (Langmuir). The surface has a fixed number of identical sites; each site holds one molecule; held molecules do not interact; adsorption stops when a single layer is complete; at equilibrium the rate of landing equals the rate of leaving.

answer.text: Derivation for a gas at partial pressure p. Let θ be the fraction of sites occupied.
answer.pre:
rate of adsorption  = k<sub>a</sub> p (1 − θ)      (molecules land only on empty sites)
rate of desorption  = k<sub>d</sub> θ             (molecules leave only from full sites)
equilibrium: k<sub>a</sub> p (1 − θ) = k<sub>d</sub> θ
θ = b p/(1 + b p),   b = k<sub>a</sub>/k<sub>d</sub>
q = q<sub>m</sub> θ = q<sub>m</sub> b p/(1 + b p)
for a liquid: q = q<sub>m</sub> K<sub>L</sub> C/(1 + K<sub>L</sub> C)

answer: Limits. At low concentration KLC ≪ 1 and q ≈ qmKLC, a straight Henry's law line. At high concentration KLC ≫ 1 and q → qm, the monolayer. Half the sites are full at C = 1/KL.

Constants from data. Rearranged, C/q = 1/(qmKL) + C/qm. Plot C/q against C: slope 1/qm, intercept 1/(qmKL). Example: data C = 0.5, 1, 2, 5 mg/L, q = 17.1, 24.0, 30.0, 35.3 mg/g give C/q = 0.0292, 0.0417, 0.0667, 0.1416 g/L; the line has slope 0.02498 and intercept 0.01671, so qm = 40.0 mg/g and KL = 0.02498/0.01671 = 1.50 L/mg. A straight plot confirms the model.

Freundlich. q = KFC1/n, an empirical equation that fits heterogeneous surfaces whose sites differ in strength. Taking logs, log q = log KF + (1/n) log C: a plot of log q against log C has slope 1/n and intercept log KF. For the data above, 1/n = 0.311 and KF = 22.7; the points curve slightly, so Langmuir fits better. Freundlich has no plateau and must not be extrapolated (it predicts 46.3 mg/g at 10 mg/L against Langmuir's 37.5).

Shape. An isotherm concave to the C axis (1/n < 1, or RL = 1/(1 + KLC0) between 0 and 1) is favourable: much is held even from dilute fluid, and fixed-bed fronts stay sharp. A linear isotherm is borderline; a concave-up one is unfavourable.

Pressure. For a gas, q depends on the partial pressure of the adsorbate p = yP, not the total pressure. Raising the total pressure at a fixed mole fraction raises p and q; adding inert gas does not. Pressure-swing adsorption loads at high pressure and regenerates at low pressure.

Temperature. Physical adsorption is exothermic, so at a fixed p or C a hotter bed holds less; constants belong to the temperature at which they were measured. Two isotherms give the heat of adsorption from the pressures needed for the same loading: if 0.10 bar at 25 °C and 0.40 bar at 60 °C give the same q, ΔHads = R ln 4/(1/298.15 − 1/333.15) = 11.53/3.523 × 10−4 = 32.7 kJ/mol, typical of physical adsorption. Temperature-swing adsorption loads cold and regenerates hot.
Check. With the fitted constants, q at C = 2 mg/L is 40 × 3/4 = 30.0 mg/g, the measured value.

bank.q: Explain the principle of ion exchange. Describe cation and anion exchange resins, selectivity, the service and regeneration cycle, and the techniques and equipment used, with applications.
outline: Batch, fixed bed, two-bed, mixed bed, continuous
answer: Principle. An ion-exchange resin carries fixed ionic groups throughout its beads, balanced by mobile counter-ions. Ions from the solution replace the counter-ions, which go into the solution, equivalent for equivalent, so the solution stays electrically neutral. Softening on a sodium-form resin: 2R–SO3Na + Ca2+ ⇌ (R–SO3)2Ca + 2Na+. One Ca2+ releases two Na+: the ion count doubles, the equivalents stay equal. The reaction is reversible, which allows regeneration.

Resins. Beads of polystyrene cross-linked with about 8 % divinylbenzene. Strong acid cation resins carry −SO3− and work at any pH; weak acid resins carry −COO− and regenerate very efficiently. Strong base anion resins carry quaternary ammonium groups and remove even silica and CO2; weak base resins carry tertiary amines and take only strong acids.

Capacity. Total capacity is the number of groups (about 1.8–2.0 eq per litre of strong acid resin); the operating capacity actually used between regenerations is lower, 0.8–1.4 eq/L, and is what sizes a bed.

Selectivity. In dilute solution a resin prefers ions of higher charge and, at equal charge, smaller hydrated size: Ba2+ > Pb2+ > Ca2+ > Mg2+ > K+ > NH4+ > Na+ > H+ for cation resins and SO42− > NO3− > Cl− > HCO3− > OH− for strong base resins. The selectivity coefficient is KA/B = yAxB/(xAyB). A concentrated regenerant overcomes the preference, which is why 10 % brine strips calcium.

Cycle. (1) Service: water flows down; an exchange zone moves down the bed as in fixed-bed adsorption, and the run ends when hardness or conductivity at the outlet rises. (2) Backwash: upflow lifts the bed, removes dirt and regrades the beads. (3) Regeneration: 8–12 % NaCl, 4–6 % HCl or 2–4 % NaOH passed slowly, usually two to three times the stoichiometric amount. (4) Rinse: excess regenerant washed out.

Co- and counter-current regeneration. In co-current regeneration the regenerant flows down like the water and the outlet end of the bed is regenerated worst, causing leakage. In counter-current regeneration the regenerant enters at the outlet end, so the cleanest resin meets the treated water last; leakage and chemical use fall.

Techniques and equipment. Batch contact in a stirred tank for small lots. Fixed-bed pressure columns with distributors and collectors, run in pairs so one serves while the other regenerates. Two-bed demineraliser: H-form cation column, degasser to strip CO2, OH-form anion column. Mixed bed: cation and anion beads mixed in one column act as many exchangers in series and give water of very low conductivity; the beads are separated by backwashing for regeneration. Continuous counter-current units move resin in pulses round service, regeneration and rinse zones.

Applications. Softening and demineralising boiler feed and process water; ultrapure water for electronics; recovery of chromium and precious metals from plating rinses; uranium from leach liquors; sugar decolourising; purification of antibiotics such as streptomycin; removal of radioactive caesium; solid acid catalysts.
Check with numbers. 500 L/h of water with 4.0 meq/L hardness for 8 h is 16 eq; at 1.0 eq/L this needs 16 L of resin, and 150 g/L of salt is 2.4 kg, 2.57 times the stoichiometric 935 g.

bank.q: Explain solubility curves, supersaturation and Miers' supersaturation theory. List the methods of creating supersaturation and describe the kinds of nucleation.
outline: Primary homogeneous, heterogeneous and secondary nucleation
answer: Solubility curve. Solubility is the concentration of a solution in equilibrium with the solid, usually in g of solute per 100 g of water, plotted against temperature. Most salts (KNO3) are much more soluble hot; NaCl hardly changes (about 36 to 39 g per 100 g water from 20 to 100 °C); a few, such as anhydrous Na2SO4 above 32.4 °C, are less soluble hot. A salt that forms hydrates has one branch per hydrate, meeting at transition points (Na2SO4·10H2O changes to Na2SO4 at 32.4 °C).

Supersaturation. A solution holding more solute than the solubility C* is supersaturated. It is measured by ΔC = C − C*, the ratio S = C/C* or the relative value σ = S − 1. For example 45 g per 100 g water where C* = 30 gives ΔC = 15, S = 1.5, σ = 0.5. Supersaturation is the driving force for both nucleation and growth.

Miers' theory. Miers showed that a clean solution can be cooled below its saturation temperature without crystallizing. He drew a supersolubility curve roughly parallel to the solubility curve. Between them lies the metastable zone, where crystals present grow but new nuclei rarely form; beyond the supersolubility curve lies the labile zone, where nuclei form on their own. Below the solubility curve the solution is unsaturated and crystals dissolve. The supersolubility curve is not fixed: faster cooling, stronger agitation and impurities move it.

Example. A solution saturated at 60 °C at 40 g per 100 g water, cooled to 20 °C where the solubility is 20 g, would reach S = 2.0 if no crystals formed: deep in the labile zone, giving a shower of fines. With seeds added just after it becomes saturated, solute deposits on the seeds and the path stays in the metastable zone. At the end, 1000 kg of feed gives 285.7 − 142.9 = 142.9 kg of crystals.

Creating supersaturation. (1) Cooling, for salts whose solubility falls with temperature. (2) Evaporating solvent, for flat-solubility salts such as NaCl. (3) Adding an antisolvent or a common-ion salt that lowers the solubility (salting-out). (4) A chemical reaction that forms a sparingly soluble product (precipitation). Vacuum crystallization combines cooling and evaporation by flashing hot feed at low pressure.

Primary homogeneous nucleation. Nuclei form from the clear solution alone. A cluster must reach the critical radius r* = 2γvm/(kT ln S) to grow; the energy barrier ΔG* falls as 1/(ln S)², so the rate is negligible until S is high and then rises steeply.
Primary heterogeneous nucleation. Nuclei form on dust, walls or stirrers, which lower the barrier, so it starts at lower supersaturation. Real solutions always contain such surfaces.

Secondary nucleation. New crystals come from crystals already present: fragments from collisions with the impeller, walls or other crystals, or layers sheared off growing faces. It works within the metastable zone and supplies most of the nuclei in stirred industrial crystallizers.
Check. In the example, S = 40/20 = 2.0 and the mass balance closes: 142.9 kg crystals + 857.1 kg mother liquor (714.3 water + 142.9 solute) = 1000 kg.

bank.q: Equilibrium tests of a pollutant on powdered carbon give C (mg/L) = 2, 5, 10, 20 and q (mg/g) = 11.31, 17.89, 25.30, 35.78. Fit the Freundlich isotherm. 2000 L of water at 40 mg/L must be brought to 4 mg/L. Find the carbon needed in one stage, in two cross-current stages at the best intermediate concentration, in two counter-current stages, and the least possible carbon.

answer.text: Freundlich fit. Take logs of the data:

answer: The points lie on a straight line. Slope = (1.554 − 1.053)/(1.301 − 0.301) = 0.501/1.000 = 0.500 = 1/n, so n = 2. Intercept: log K<sub>F</sub> = 1.053 − 0.500 × 0.301 = 0.903, K<sub>F</sub> = 8.0. Isotherm: q = 8.0C<sup>0.5</sup> (mg/g, C in mg/L).
Solute to remove. 2000 L × (40 − 4) mg/L = 72 000 mg in every case.
One stage. The carbon leaves in equilibrium with 4 mg/L: q = 8 × 40.5 = 16.0 mg/g. W = 72 000/16.0 = 4500 g = 4.50 kg.

answer.text: Two cross-current stages. Fresh carbon in each stage; total W = V(C0 − C1)/q(C1) + V(C1 − C2)/q(C2). Setting dW/dC1 = 0 for a Freundlich isotherm gives (C1/C2)1/n − (1/n)(C0/C1) = 1 − 1/n. Solve by trial:

Two counter-current stages. Fresh carbon enters stage 2 (where the water leaves at 4 mg/L) and leaves stage 1 loaded to q(C1). Overall: V(C0 − C2) = Wq(C1); stage 2: V(C1 − C2) = Wq(C2). Dividing: (C0 − C2)/q(C1) = (C1 − C2)/q(C2).

answer: Least carbon. With infinitely many counter-current stages the carbon leaves in equilibrium with the feed: q(40) = 8 × 6.325 = 50.6 mg/g, Wmin = 72 000/50.6 = 1423 g.

answer.text: Comparison.

answer: Conclusion. Two counter-current stages need 45 % of the single-stage carbon and 67 % of the cross-current carbon, because the carbon leaves in contact with the strongest liquid. Check: every scheme removes 72 000 mg.

bank.q: A carbon bed 1.0 m deep holding 20 kg of carbon treats 1.0 m³/h of water containing 100 mg/L of an organic. Outlet readings are: t (h) 0, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14 and C/C<sub>0</sub> 0, 0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.12, 0.25, 0.45, 0.66, 0.82, 0.92, 0.97, 1.00. The break point is C/C<sub>0</sub> = 0.05. Find the loading at the break point and at saturation, the fraction of the bed used, the LUB, and the bed depth for a 12 h run at the same velocity. Explain how a higher flow rate would change the result.
answer: Break time. C/C0 reaches 0.05 at tb = 5 h.

answer.text: Area above the curve, ∫(1 − C/C0)dt, by trapezoids:

answer: Loadings. C0Q = 100 g/m³ × 1.0 m³/h = 100 g/h. Held at the break point = 100 × 4.945 = 494.5 g, so qb = 494.5/20 = 24.7 g/kg (mg/g). Stoichiometric time ts = 8.245 h; held at saturation = 824.5 g, qsat = 41.2 mg/g, the loading in equilibrium with 100 mg/L.
Fraction used and LUB. At the break point the bed has used 494.5/824.5 = 60 % of its capacity. LUB = H(1 − tb/ts) = 1.0 × (1 − 5/8.245) = 0.394 m.

Scale-up. Each metre of fully used bed lasts ts/H = 8.245 h. For tb = 12 h the used length is 12/8.245 = 1.455 m, and the LUB is unchanged at the same velocity and particle size: H = 1.455 + 0.394 = 1.85 m. Check: ts = 8.245 × 1.85 = 15.25 h, tb = 15.25 × (1 − 0.394/1.85) = 12.0 h. The new bed holds 37 kg of carbon and uses 79 % of it at the break point.
Shortcut to avoid. C0Qtb/W = 100 × 5/20 = 25.0 mg/g counts all the solute fed up to 5 h as held; the curve shows a little leaked, so integrate.

Higher flow rate. At a higher velocity the solute arrives faster and has less contact time per unit length, so the mass-transfer zone widens: the curve becomes flatter, tb comes earlier by more than the ratio of the flows, the LUB grows and a smaller fraction of the carbon is used at the break point. The saturation loading qsat does not change, since it is an equilibrium value. Lead–lag operation of two beds in series recovers the unused part by running the first bed to exhaustion.

bank.q: Design a sodium-cycle softener for 10 m³/h of boiler make-up water with hardness 250 mg/L as CaCO<sub>3</sub>, for a 12 h run. The resin's operating capacity is 1.1 eq/L, the service velocity 20 m/h and the salt dose 160 g NaCl per litre of resin. Find the equivalents per run, the resin volume, the column diameter and bed depth, the salt per regeneration and its ratio to the stoichiometric amount, and the 10 % brine used.
answer: Hardness. 1 meq/L = 50.04 mg/L as CaCO3, so 250/50.04 = 5.00 meq/L.
Load per run. Water per run = 10 m³/h × 12 h = 120 m³ = 120 000 L. Equivalents = 120 000 × 5.00 meq/L = 600 000 meq = 600 eq (that is 300 mol of Ca2+ and Mg2+ exchanged for 600 mol of Na+).
Resin volume. VR = 600 eq/1.1 eq/L = 545 L = 0.545 m³.

answer.text: Column.
answer.pre:
area A = flow/velocity = 10/20 = 0.50 m²
diameter D = (4A/π)<sup>0.5</sup> = (4 × 0.50/3.1416)<sup>0.5</sup> = 0.80 m
bed depth = V<sub>R</sub>/A = 0.545/0.50 = 1.09 m

answer: A depth of about 1.1 m is within the usual 0.75–2 m; the vessel is made about 1.6 times the bed depth so the bed can expand during backwash.

answer.text: Regeneration.
answer.pre:
salt = 160 g/L × 545 L = 87 200 g = 87.2 kg
stoichiometric salt = 600 eq × 58.44 g/eq = 35 060 g = 35.1 kg
ratio = 87.2/35.1 = 2.49  (regenerant efficiency 40 %)
10 % brine = 87.2/0.10 = 872 kg per regeneration

answer: Operation. Two columns are installed so that one serves while the other is backwashed, regenerated (brine passed slowly, typically over 20–40 min) and rinsed. Counter-current regeneration would cut the salt and the hardness leakage. The product water carries 5.00 meq/L of sodium in place of the hardness, 115 mg/L of Na+, which is acceptable for low-pressure boilers; high-pressure boilers need demineralised water from a two-bed or mixed-bed unit.

answer.text: Regeneration steps sized.
answer.pre:
backwash: 15 m/h upflow for 10 min = 0.50 × 15 × 10/60 = 1.25 m³ of water
brine: 872 kg at about 1071 kg/m³ = 0.81 m³, passed at 4 bed volumes per hour
       = 4 × 0.545 = 2.18 m³/h, so it takes 0.81/2.18 h = 22 min
rinse: 3–5 bed volumes = 1.6–2.7 m³ of water

answer: Sensitivity. The run time is capacity divided by load: if the hardness rose to 300 mg/L as CaCO3 (6.0 meq/L), the same bed would last 600/(10 × 6.0) = 10 h, so the run is controlled by a hardness meter on the outlet rather than by the clock. A lower salt dose (say 100 g/L) raises the regenerant efficiency but lowers the operating capacity, so the bed must be larger; the design trades salt cost against resin volume.
Check. Capacity 545 L × 1.1 eq/L = 600 eq = load per run; salt ratio 2.49 lies in the usual range of 2–3.

bank.q: 5000 kg/h of sodium sulfate solution holding 32 g Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> per 100 g water at 30 °C is cooled to 15 °C in a continuous cooling crystallizer, where the solubility is 13.0 g per 100 g water. The crystals are Glauber's salt, Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>·10H<sub>2</sub>O (Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> 142.04, H<sub>2</sub>O 18.015). Take c<sub>p</sub> = 3.6 kJ/(kg K) and a heat of crystallization of 240 kJ per kg of hydrate. Cooling water enters at 10 °C and leaves at 18 °C, counter-current, with U = 0.45 kW/(m² K). Find the crystals, the yield, the heat removed, the cooling water and the area.
answer: Feed. Na2SO4 = 5000 × 32/132 = 1212.1 kg/h; water = 3787.9 kg/h. At 30 °C the solubility (about 40 g per 100 g) exceeds 32, so the feed is unsaturated and no crystals form before cooling.

answer.text: Balance. Let H kg/h of hydrate form. The mother liquor keeps 3787.9 − 0.5591H of water, holding 0.130 times that of salt.

answer: Yield. Na2SO4 in crystals = 0.4409 × 1954.8 = 861.8 kg/h, 71.1 % of the feed salt. Had the crystals been anhydrous at the same solubility, only 1212.1 − 492.4 = 719.7 kg/h (59.4 %) would form: the 1093 kg/h of water locked in the hydrate leaves less water to hold salt.
Check. Mother liquor = 5000 − 1954.8 = 3045.2 kg/h, holding 2694.9 kg/h water and 350.3 kg/h Na2SO4: 350.3/2694.9 = 0.130 ✓.

answer.text: Heat removed.

answer: The heat of crystallization is 63 % of the duty here, because Glauber's salt dissolves with a large heat absorption; leaving it out would undersize the cooler almost threefold.

answer.text: Area.

answer: Magma density. The crystals are 1954.8/5000 = 39 % of the outlet mass, a thick slurry. Part of the mother liquor is usually recycled to the crystallizer to keep the solids near 20–30 % so the magma can be pumped and the crystals do not break.

Purity and handling. The hydrate crystals carry adhering mother liquor (13 g Na2SO4 per 100 g water plus any impurities), so they are centrifuged and washed with a little cold water. They must be dried below 32.4 °C, or they melt in their own water of crystallization; where anhydrous product is wanted, the decahydrate is melted and the anhydrous salt crystallized by evaporation above 32.4 °C.

Comment. The small temperature differences limit scaling on the cold surface; a jacket alone could not provide 57 m², so an external cooler with circulating magma, or a Swenson–Walker trough train, would be used.

bank.q: Derive the MSMPR population density relation. A sodium chloride MSMPR crystallizer (ρ = 2160 kg/m³, k<sub>v</sub> = 1) with τ = 1.5 h gives population densities 1.027 × 10<sup>10</sup>, 2.707 × 10<sup>9</sup>, 7.135 × 10<sup>8</sup> and 1.881 × 10<sup>8</sup> per (m³ mm) at L = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 mm. Find G, n°, B°, N<sub>T</sub>, M<sub>T</sub> and L<sub>D</sub>. Predict L<sub>D</sub> if τ is doubled at the same magma density, with B° = k<sub>N</sub>G<sup>3</sup>.
answer: Assumptions. Steady state; well-mixed magma; product withdrawn with the vessel's CSD; crystal-free feed; no breakage or agglomeration; growth independent of size (ΔL law).

answer.text: Balance on crystals between L and L + ΔL in magma volume V over Δt:
answer.pre:
in by growth  − out by growth        = out with product
V G n(L) Δt   − V G n(L + ΔL) Δt    = Q n ΔL Δt
divide by ΔL Δt, let ΔL → 0:  V G dn/dL = −Q n
with τ = V/Q:  dn/dL = −n/(Gτ)  ⇒  n = n° exp(−L/Gτ),  ln n = ln n° − L/(Gτ)

answer.text: Data.
Rates and moments.
answer.pre:
B° = n°G = 2.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> × 0.100 = 2.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> nuclei/(m³ h)
N<sub>T</sub> = n°Gτ = 2.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> × 0.150 = 3.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> crystals/m³
M<sub>T</sub> = 6 k<sub>v</sub> ρ n° (Gτ)<sup>4</sup>, n° = 2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> per (m³ m), Gτ = 1.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m
     = 6 × 1 × 2160 × 2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> × 5.06 × 10<sup>−16</sup> = 131 kg/m³
L<sub>D</sub> = 3Gτ = 0.45 mm; number mean 0.15 mm; mass-weighted mean 0.60 mm

answer.text: Doubling τ at fixed MT. With B° = kNG3, n° = B°/G = kNG2, so MT ∝ G2(Gτ)4 = G6τ4. Fixed MT gives G ∝ τ−2/3.

answer: Conclusion. Doubling the residence time (a vessel twice as large for the same feed) lowers the supersaturation, cuts nucleation fourfold and G by 37 %, and raises the dominant size only from 0.45 to 0.57 mm, a factor 21/3 = 1.26. Larger gains need fines destruction or classified product removal.

bank.q: A brackish-water RO plant receives 50 m³/h at 3500 mg/L NaCl and 25 °C, runs at 80 % recovery and 98 % salt rejection, at ΔP = 20 bar, with A<sub>w</sub> = 2.5 L/(m² h bar). Find the permeate and concentrate flows and concentrations, the osmotic pressures, the net driving pressure, the flux and the membrane area, and the number of 37 m² elements. Repeat the flux with a concentration polarisation factor of 1.2 on the feed side.

answer.text: Flows.
Osmotic pressures, π = 2CRT with C in mol/m³ (NaCl 58.44 g/mol):

answer: Net driving pressure. The feed side changes from 2.97 to 14.60 bar along the module; using the mean, 8.78 bar, Δπ = 8.78 − 0.059 = 8.72 bar. Net = 20 − 8.72 = 11.28 bar.

Flux and area. Jw = 2.5 × 11.28 = 28.2 L/(m² h). Area = 40 000 L/h/28.2 = 1419 m². Elements = 1419/37 = 38.4, so 39 elements, for example in pressure vessels of six or seven elements in two stages (tapered array) so that the flow along the later elements stays high.

With polarisation. The salt at the membrane is 1.2 times the bulk, so the feed-side π rises to 1.2 × 8.78 = 10.54 bar: net = 20 − (10.54 − 0.06) = 9.52 bar, Jw = 23.8 L/(m² h), area = 40 000/23.8 = 1681 m², 46 elements. Polarisation costs 16 % of the flux and also raises the salt passage and the scaling risk at the concentrate end, where 17 220 mg/L may exceed the solubility of CaSO4 or CaCO3; antiscalant dosing and acid are used.

Salt passage. Salt reaching the permeate = 40 m³/h × 70 g/m³ = 2.8 kg/h, or 2800/1419 = 1.97 g/(m² h). With a mean feed-side concentration of about (3500 + 17 220)/2 = 10 360 mg/L, the salt permeability is B = Js/(Cm − Cp) = 1.97/10 290 = 1.9 × 10−4 m/h. Since Js does not depend on pressure while Jw does, a higher ΔP gives more water for the same salt, that is purer permeate; a lower ΔP or a fouled membrane gives saltier permeate.

Temperature. Aw rises by roughly 3 % per °C because water becomes less viscous, so a cold-season feed at 15 °C needs either more pressure or more elements; B rises too, so permeate salt also rises in summer.
Energy. Pump power ≈ QΔP/η = (50/3600) × 20 × 105/0.8 = 34.7 kW, or 0.87 kWh per m³ of permeate without energy recovery.

Check. Salt in = 175 kg/h; out = 40 × 0.070 + 10 × 17.22 = 2.8 + 172.2 = 175.0 kg/h ✓. The net pressure (11.3 bar) is positive at the concentrate end too: 20 − 14.6 = 5.4 bar, so water is still pushed through the last element.

bank.q: A continuous crystallizer makes a product that is too fine. Analyse how supersaturation, residence time, seeding, agitation, fines destruction and the type of crystallizer affect the crystal size, and recommend changes, using the MSMPR relations where you can.
outline: Why fines form: B and G orders
Effect of τ at fixed magma density
answer: Starting point. The product size is set by the competition between nucleation, B° = kNσb, and growth, G = kgσg. Since b (2–9) is usually larger than g (1–2), a higher supersaturation raises nucleation more than growth, so the solute is shared among more crystals and each stays small. A fine product means either too high a supersaturation or too much secondary nucleation.

Residence time. In an MSMPR crystallizer LD = 3Gτ. Writing B° = kNGi (i = b/g) and holding the magma density fixed gives G ∝ τ−4/(i+3) and LD ∝ τ(i−1)/(i+3). For i = 3, doubling τ (a vessel twice the size) raises LD by 21/3 = 1.26; for i = 2 only by 21/5 = 1.15. A longer τ helps, but it is an expensive way to gain size. Lowering supersaturation at a fixed τ by itself lowers G and does not enlarge the crystals unless nucleation falls further.

Seeding and supersaturation control. In batch work, seeding just inside the metastable zone and cooling slowly at first keeps σ low and lets the seeds take up the solute; by the ΔL law, 1 kg of 0.1 mm seed grown to 0.5 mm becomes 125 kg of product. In continuous work, a high magma density (20–40 % solids) gives a large crystal surface that consumes supersaturation quickly and keeps σ low.

Agitation. Agitation speeds the diffusion step of growth but also causes contact nucleation and breakage, which are the main source of nuclei in stirred vessels. A slow, large impeller, lower tip speed and a pump that does not crush crystals cut secondary nucleation; the stirring needs to be just enough to suspend the crystals.

Fines destruction. Drawing liquor from a quiet zone where only small crystals are carried, heating it to dissolve them and returning it removes surplus nuclei. Fewer crystals share the same solute, so they grow larger. This is what a draft-tube baffle (DTB) crystallizer does. Classified product removal (withdrawing only the larger crystals, as in an Oslo unit) raises the size and narrows the spread further; both make the ln n plot depart from the MSMPR straight line.

Crystallizer type. A forced-circulation unit with a high circulation rate through a pump and heater gives fine to medium crystals and high capacity; a DTB with fines destruction gives coarser crystals; an Oslo (classifying) crystallizer grows crystals in a fluidised bed with gentle supersaturated flow and gives the largest, most even product.

Heat transfer and scaling. In cooling crystallizers a large wall temperature difference makes local high supersaturation, nucleation and scale. Keeping the wall ΔT below about 10 °C, or using vacuum cooling with no cold surface, helps.

Recommendation. For a continuous duty now in a forced-circulation unit: convert to a DTB with fines destruction, keep magma density high, reduce impeller or pump tip speed, and only then consider a longer τ. Check: with i = 3 the MSMPR prediction for doubling τ (0.45 to 0.57 mm in the bank's MSMPR example) shows that size gains from τ alone are small, so nuclei removal is the stronger lever.

bank.q: Compare reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration, electrodialysis and liquid membranes in driving force, membrane, what is separated and limitations. Choose a process, with reasons, for (a) brackish water to drinking water, (b) concentrating whey proteins, (c) recovering copper from a dilute leach liquor.
outline: What passes and what is held

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Feature
Reverse osmosis
Ultrafiltration
Electrodialysis
Liquid membrane
rows: concentration difference, often of a counter-ion
organic liquid in a porous support or as emulsion skin, with carrier
carrier binds and releases the solute
energy rises with salt removed; limiting current

answer: RO needs ΔP greater than the osmotic pressure, Jw = Aw(ΔP − Δπ); for 2000 mg/L NaCl π = 1.70 bar, for seawater about 27 bar. It removes nearly every dissolved species and bacteria, but the concentrate may scale and the membranes foul, so pretreatment (often UF) is needed.

UF sieves by size at low pressure; beyond the gel point the flux follows J = k ln(Cg/Cb) and is raised by cross-flow, not pressure. With k = 1.0 × 10−5 m/s, Cg = 250 g/L and Cb = 10 g/L, J = 116 L/(m² h).

ED moves only ions, with a current I = zFQΔC/(εN): 1 m³/h desalted from 2000 to 500 mg/L in 100 cell pairs at ε = 0.9 needs 7.6 A and, at 120 V, 0.92 kWh/m³. Its energy rises with the salt removed, so it suits moderate salinity; it leaves neutral organics and microbes in the product.

Liquid membranes carry a chosen solute uphill by coupling it to a counter-flow of another ion, so a dilute feed can give a concentrated strip solution; they are highly selective but the organic liquid slowly leaks out.

(a) Brackish water to drinking water. RO, or ED/EDR. RO also removes microbes, organics and neutral species such as silica and is the usual choice; EDR is competitive below about 3000 mg/L and tolerates silica and scaling better. Choose RO with UF or cartridge pretreatment for a drinking-water duty, because it gives a barrier to microbes.

(b) Whey proteins. UF with a 10 kDa membrane holds the proteins and passes lactose and salts; diafiltration (adding water) washes out more lactose. RO would concentrate everything together and ED does not concentrate neutral proteins.

(c) Copper from dilute leach liquor. A supported or emulsion liquid membrane with a copper-selective carrier (an oxime as used in solvent extraction) moves Cu2+ into a strong acid strip solution, concentrating it and leaving iron behind; RO would concentrate every ion, and ED would not discriminate between copper and other cations.
Check. Each choice matches the species to the property the membrane uses: size for UF, charge for ED, chemical affinity for the liquid membrane and solubility–diffusion for RO.

bank.q: A dye house discharges 20 m³/h of wastewater with 30 mg/L of dye, hardness 300 mg/L as CaCO<sub>3</sub> and 1500 mg/L of dissolved salts. The plant wants to reuse it as low-pressure boiler feed. Propose and evaluate a treatment train using adsorption, ion exchange and membranes: choose the adsorbent and contactor, size the carbon use and the softener, decide where RO fits, and state what must be checked by tests.
answer: Targets. Low-pressure boiler feed needs nearly zero hardness, low dissolved solids and no colour or organics that foam or foul. The water has three problems: dye (organic, coloured), hardness (scale) and dissolved salt.
Pretreatment. Settling or filtration removes suspended solids that would blind carbon and resin beds; a sand or cartridge filter (or UF) protects the later units.

Dye removal. Dyes are large organic molecules, so a non-polar, mesoporous activated carbon is chosen: its mesopores admit the dye and its area gives high capacity. Granular carbon in two fixed beds in lead–lag series is preferred to powdered carbon in stirred tanks: the first bed can be run to exhaustion while the second polishes, so the carbon is used nearly to its saturation loading and the effluent stays below 1 mg/L.

answer.text: Carbon use. Suppose column tests give a loading at the break point of 60 mg/g for this dye (to be measured).
answer.pre:
dye removed = 20 m³/h × (30 − 1) g/m³ = 580 g/h = 13.9 kg/day
carbon used = 13.9 kg/day/0.060 kg/kg = 232 kg/day
with lead–lag running each bed nearer saturation, less (perhaps 150–180 kg/day)

answer: Spent carbon is regenerated thermally off site; dye does not desorb easily with steam.

answer.text: Softening. Hardness 300 mg/L as CaCO3 = 300/50.04 = 6.0 meq/L. A sodium-form strong acid resin, regenerated with brine, two columns.
answer.pre:
load = 20 m³/h × 6.0 eq/m³ = 120 eq/h = 2880 eq/day
8 h run: 960 eq; at 1.0 eq/L operating capacity: 960 L of resin per column
salt at 2.5 × stoichiometric: 2.5 × 960 × 58.44 g = 140 kg per regeneration

answer: Salt removal. 1500 mg/L of dissolved solids is too high for boiler feed even after softening, which only swaps calcium for sodium. Two options: (i) RO after softening, at 75 % recovery giving 15 m³/h of permeate with about 2–3 % of the salt; softening first prevents CaCO3 and CaSO4 scale in the RO concentrate; (ii) a two-bed demineraliser on the full flow, which at 1500 mg/L (about 25 meq/L) would need very large resin volumes and regenerant, so it is used only to polish the RO permeate if a higher-pressure boiler is later added.

Order. Filter → carbon (lead–lag) → softener → RO → (optional mixed bed). Carbon goes before the resin and the membrane because dye and other organics foul both; softening goes before RO to prevent scale.

Wastes. Spent carbon (to regeneration), brine from the softener (about 140 kg of salt per regeneration plus hardness), and RO concentrate, 5 m³/h at about 6000 mg/L. These must be discharged or evaporated; their cost often decides between RO and a demineraliser.

Evaluation. The train meets the target with mature equipment; carbon cost and concentrate disposal are the largest running costs. An alternative is nanofiltration in place of softener plus RO, which removes hardness and colour together but passes much of the monovalent salt; it would suit a less strict reuse.

Tests needed. Isotherm and small-column breakthrough tests for the dye on the chosen carbon (to fix the 60 mg/g assumption and the LUB); the resin's operating capacity at this water's hardness and sodium; RO scaling indices and a pilot run for fouling; and the boiler's actual feedwater limits.
Check. Carbon removes 13.9 kg/day of dye; the softener removes 2880 eq/day of hardness; RO delivers 15 m³/h, enough for a boiler raising about 14 t/h of steam.

glossary.def: The solute held on the surface of the adsorbent.
The porous solid that holds the solute, such as activated carbon or a zeolite.
Outlet concentration against time (or volume) for a fixed bed.
The time at which the outlet concentration reaches the allowed limit and the bed is switched.
The band of a fixed bed in which the fluid concentration falls from the feed value to nearly zero.
LUB = H(1 − t<sub>b</sub>/t<sub>s</sub>), the part of a bed not yet used at the break point.
Equilibrium loading against fluid concentration or partial pressure at one temperature.
q<sub>m</sub>, the Langmuir loading when every site holds one molecule.
A zeolite or carbon with uniform pores close to molecular size.
The equivalents an ion-exchange bed delivers between regenerations.
Restoring an adsorbent or resin by heat, pressure drop or a chemical (brine, acid, alkali).
K<sub>A/B</sub> = y<sub>A</sub>x<sub>B</sub>/(x<sub>A</sub>y<sub>B</sub>), the preference of a resin for ion A over B.
Cation and anion resins mixed in one column to make very pure water.
The outward shape of a crystal, which changes with growth conditions.
One of two or more crystal lattices of the same substance.
Concentration above the solubility; ΔC = C − C*, S = C/C*.
Region above the solubility curve where crystals grow but few nuclei form.
Region beyond the supersolubility curve where nuclei form spontaneously.
Formation of new crystals from crystals already present, by contact or shear.
The cluster size at the top of the free-energy barrier; smaller clusters dissolve.
The suspension of crystals in mother liquor inside a crystallizer.
The saturated solution left after crystals are removed.
Number of crystals per unit size range per unit volume, n = dN/dL.
The size at which the mass distribution peaks; 3Gτ in an MSMPR crystallizer.
The stream that passes a membrane and the stream held back.
Build-up of rejected solute at the membrane surface.
The molar mass of solute that an ultrafiltration membrane rejects to 90 %.
In electrodialysis, one cation membrane, diluate, anion membrane and concentrate compartment.
